content: Psychological and behavioral issues are frequently observed in children and adolescents. Enhancing self-esteem in this population may play a critical role in preventing the onset of such problems. While there is robust evidence supporting the physical health benefits of exercise, the impact of exercise on mental health, particularly self-esteem, remains less well-documented. The primary objective of this research was to evaluate whether exercise alone, or exercise as part of a broader intervention, can effectively improve self-esteem in children and young people. To achieve this, comprehensive searches were conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, The Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (CENTRAL), CINAHL, PsycINFO, and ERIC. Additionally, reference lists from relevant articles were reviewed, and authors of studies were contacted to identify further relevant research. The most recent searches were completed in May 2003 for CENTRAL and January 2002 for the other databases. The inclusion criteria for the studies were as follows: randomized controlled trials involving children and young people aged 3 to 20 years, with at least one intervention group engaging in gross motor activity for a duration exceeding four weeks, and self-esteem being the primary outcome measure. Two independent reviewers were responsible for selecting the studies, assessing their validity, and extracting the relevant data. When necessary, investigators were contacted to retrieve missing data or clarify ambiguities. A total of 23 trials, encompassing 1,821 children and young people, were included in the analysis. Most of these trials were small in scale, and only one was determined to have a low risk of bias. Thirteen of the trials compared exercise alone to no intervention. Eight of these trials were included in a meta-analysis, but the results were heterogeneous. Among these, one study with a low risk of bias demonstrated a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 1.33 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.43 to 2.23). In contrast, the SMD for three studies with a moderate risk of bias was 0.21 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.59), and for four studies with a high risk of bias, the SMD was 0.57 (95% CI 0.11 to 1.04). Twelve trials investigated the effects of exercise as part of a comprehensive intervention compared to no intervention. However, only four of these trials provided sufficient data to calculate overall effects. The results from these studies suggest a moderate short-term improvement in self-esteem favoring the intervention, with an SMD of 0.51 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.88). In conclusion, the findings suggest that exercise has a positive short-term impact on self-esteem in children and young people. Given the absence of known adverse effects of exercise and its numerous physical health benefits, incorporating exercise into interventions aimed at improving self-esteem in this population appears to be a valuable strategy. However, it is important to note that these conclusions are based on several small trials of low methodological quality.
